title: How to Transcend the Torment of Self-Focus
author: Arthur Brooks
summary: Arthur Brooks identifies excessive self-focus as a natural but happiness-undermining tendency that humans must consciously override. Drawing on Augustine's homo incurvatus in se ('being curved in on oneself') and a 2002 meta-analysis of over 200 studies showing a strong positive correlation between self-focused attention and negative emotions, Brooks argues that Mother Nature's evolutionary wiring works against flourishing. He offers three science-backed practices to counteract self-focus: focusing on bringing happiness to others (creating emotional contagion), engaging in small generous acts (defocusing the self), and practicing mindfulness (interrupting retrospective and prospective self-referential thinking). The piece combines personal honesty with research-grounded guidance, illustrating how even happiness scholars must fight their own wiring.
points: * Excessive self-focus is evolutionarily natural but psychologically harmful; a 2002 meta-analysis of 200+ studies found a strong positive correlation between self-focused attention and negative emotions. * Augustine diagnosed this tendency as homo incurvatus in se -- 'a state of being curved in on oneself' -- leading to 'restless discomfort with life and a permanent state of dissatisfaction.' * Three proven remedies: (1) focus on bringing happiness to others via emotional contagion, (2) engage in small generous acts that defocus the self, and (3) practice mindfulness to interrupt self-referential rumination. * Self-referential thinking is typically retrospective and prospective -- ruminating on past and future -- which is why present-focused practices are effective counterweights. * The path is not heroic self-erasure but consistent, small practices of attention toward others: picking up litter, donating to charity, helping a neighbor. * Brooks is candid about his own wiring: 'I am a specialist in the science of happiness... But here's my honest answer: candy corn and cigarettes' -- illustrating that knowing the truth doesn't exempt us from the fight.
quotes: Mother Nature doesn't care about your happiness at all. Many of our natural urges, in fact, lead us in exactly the opposite direction from the bliss we seek.

Early Christian writers, such as Saint Augustine in the fourth century, called this tendency homo incurvatus in se, a state of being that involves being curved in on oneself, or ingrown, leading to a restless discomfort with life.
Almost nothing brings greater misery than an obsessive self-focus.

When you are looking for ways to help another, you are distracted from your own preoccupations and problems; second, by bringing happiness to someone else, you can 'catch' that happiness through what behavioral scientists call emotional contagion.
